```{r setup}
library(LinearModel625)
library(bench)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
```

## Simple Profile

We can examine the run time and memory profile of my implementation of the linear
model vs stats::lm() using the library bench and the following small simulated dataset.

```{r basic_sim}
set.seed(123)
n <- 1000
x1 <- rnorm(n, 3, 1)
x2 <- rnorm(n, 10, 3)
eps <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)
y <- 2 + 0.7 * x1 + 0.35 * x2 + eps
sim_df <- data.frame(y = y, var1 = x1, var2 = x2)
  
same_coef <- function(a, b) isTRUE(all.equal(unname(coef(a)), unname(coef(b))))

results <- bench::mark(
  mod_625 <- lm(y~.,sim_df),
  mod_stats <- stats::lm(y~.,sim_df),
  check = same_coef
)

print(results)

```

As expected because both methods use optimize QR decomposition as their main mathematical
function calls we could expect them to perform similarly. We can see that this is
true for both memory allocation and total_time for this very simple benchmark. My
tests are meant to check whether these two methods produce the same estimates for
their beta matrices but we can also show here that they produce the same coefficients
vector.

The two outputs have slightly different structures as my QR decomposition returns
the R matrix while stats::lm() layers the a qr object within the S3 lm object
I wanted same performance on solution not an exact replica of stats::lm()'s
object oriented structure as I felt that would be outside the scope of this homework.
However, we can see that the main outputs of a linear model fit are all the same
between my method and stats::lm().

```{r}

coef(mod_625) == coef(mod_stats)

# all of these pieces between the models also match
all(mod_stats$residuals == mod_625$residuals)
all(mod_stats$fitted.values == mod_625$fitted.values)
all(mod_stats$rank == mod_625$rank)
all(mod_stats$df.residual == mod_625$df.residual)
all(mod_stats$terms == mod_625$terms)
all(mod_stats$model == mod_625$model)

```

## A Heavier Benchmark

We could do a more thorough testing with a function to repeatedly generate random
data and try to fit that.

```{r bench_press, eval=FALSE}
# data generated outside of package build on an AMD Ryzen 5 5600G
# this is the simulation used to create benchmark_results.rds

sim_data <- function(n, p, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("x", seq_len(p))))
  data.frame(y = drop(X %*% rnorm(p)) + rnorm(n), X)
}

# we can also show that they return the same estimates for all of this data
same_coef <- function(a, b) isTRUE(all.equal(unname(coef(a)), unname(coef(b))))

# bench::press() allows us to aggregate the data across runs with different parameters
# of bench::mark()
# here we check across a factorial design of 3 sample sizes and a set of 5 or 20 
# random covariates
results <- bench::press(
  n    = c(1e2, 1e3, 1e4),
  p    = c(5, 20),
  seed = 123:128,
  {
    df <- sim_data(n, p, seed)
    
    # generate the random data sets and then time them
    bench::mark(
      lm_625  = lm(y ~ ., data = df),
      stats = stats::lm(y ~ ., data = df),
      check = same_coef,
      min_iterations = 10
    )
  }
)

```

```{r bench_load, echo=FALSE}
results <- readRDS("benchmark_results.rds")
```

```{r bench_viz}
# Aggregate across the seeds: median of the per-dataset medians
results |>
  dplyr::mutate(expr = as.character(expression)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(n, p, expr) |> 
  dplyr::summarise(
    median_ms = median(as.numeric(median)) * 1000,
    mem_MB    = median(as.numeric(mem_alloc)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = expr, values_from = c(median_ms, mem_MB))

```

We can see that my function seems to be performing on par with stats::lm() for low
to medium sample size parameter combinations, but it's run time seems to be inflating
with my larger parameter trials. This would indicate to me that I have something
in my lm.R code that could be optimized by transitioning it into the qr decomposition
function. However, I think it is overall a succesfull test in generating a useable
package.
